To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the HlyU protein of V. cholera, a transcriptional activator of the hlyA gene, binds to an 17-bp palindrome DNA site and activates the transcription of the target gene.
HlyU, the transcriptional activator of hlyA gene, binds to an imperfect palindrome sequence, which is essential for hlyA promoter activation and virulence of V. cholera.
HlyU binds to a 17-bps palindrome sequence, and the protein dimer binds to the major grooves of the target DNA with the β-sheet wings of the protein interacting with the minor grooves of the DNA.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identification of the DNA binding sequence and characterization of the DNA binding properties of HlyU from Vibrio cholera, and suggests a redox control mechanism for HlyU.
the identification of the DNA binding site and DNA–protein interaction features of HlyA in V. cholerea, which may be important in the regulation of virulence genes in other pathogenic vibrios.

the identification of DNA binding sequence and DNA–protein interface and the dynamics of HlyU and its target DNA, which may be useful for designing drugs to control hlyA and other HlyU-regulated genes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HlyU binds to a 17-bps palindrome sequence, 173 bp 5′ to the hlyA promoter in V. cholerea, as a dimer and activates the promoter.
HlyU is a transcriptional activator of the hlyA gene in V. cholereae, which binds to its target sequence as a dimer and enhances the promoter activity.
HlyU is a dimeric DNA binding protein that recognizes the hlyA promoter and activates its expression.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HlyU binds to the target sequence in a redox-dependent manner, and that the DNA-binding domain and dimerization domain of the protein are essential for its function.
the DNA binding site for HlyU is 173 bp upstream hlyA promoter.
the DNA sequence, 5'-TAATTCAGA-3' is essential for HlyU binding, and that the redox switch may be an important mechanism in the regulation of HlyU activity.
The main takeaway from our work is that

HlyU, like many other transcriptional regulators, binds to its cognate DNA as a dimer, with its β-sheet wings contacting the minor grooves and the recognition helices, the major grooves of DNA, and that a redox switch is likely for hlyA regulation in V. chol erae.
the HlyU protein binds to its target sequence in a sequence-specific manner and the protein–DNA interaction is important for the regulation of hlyA expression.

the DNA binding and regulatory mechanisms of HlyU are similar to other winged helix–turn–helix proteins, and that the redox control in the protein might be an additional layer in regulation of hlyA expression.
